mainTopic: Caring for a מת on שבת, closing the eyes of the dying, and aggadic teachings on life versus death, poverty as a turning wheel, compassion, and tears and eyesight in old age.
overview: This amud begins with the end of the משנה: on שבת you may tie a dead person's jaw or prop up a cracked beam, but only to stop things from getting worse, not to fix them. The גמרא explains why you may rinse and oil a מת even though רבי מאיר forbade rinsing a floor: a floor can be confused with a dirt floor, but a body cannot. The word ״כל״ in the משנה adds cooling the stomach and sealing the body's openings, and verses from קהלת and מלאכי describe the stomach bursting after death. A new משנה forbids closing the eyes of the dead on שבת, and on any day while the person is dying, because that is like snuffing out a flickering candle. Then a series of teachings contrasts the living and the dead. We break שבת for a living baby but not for the dead דוד המלך, and animals fear a living baby but not the dead עוג. The גמרא urges doing מצוות while you still can and teaches that poverty is a turning wheel, so you should give to the poor and show compassion. It closes by returning to קהלת's images of old age, the effect of tears on eyesight after forty, and the story of רבי חנינא, who did not cry for his daughter so as not to lose his sight. The list of six kinds of tears continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Tying the jaw of the dead, only to stop it from opening further
steps.stepSummary: The משנה allows tying a מת's jaw on שבת. The tying may only stop the jaw from dropping more. It may not lift the jaw back into place.
steps.simpleTranslation: …so that it will delay (the body's decay). One may tie the jaw, not so that it will go up, but so that it will not open more.
steps.whatsHappening: We are joining the משנה in the middle. It first finishes a sentence about delaying the body's decay. Then it rules that you may tie a dead person's jaw on שבת, but only to keep it from opening more.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The key idea is 'hold it where it is' versus 'fix it.' Tying to stop more damage is allowed. Actively pushing the jaw back up counts as moving the body itself, and that is not allowed (a מת is מוקצה).

keyTerms.meaning: so that it will delay / hold off (the body's decay)
not so that it goes back up
so that it will not continue (to get worse)

steps.confusionAlert: The first word, שֶׁיַּמְתִּין, is not part of the jaw rule. It ends the משנה's earlier sentence about cooling the body to delay its decay.

phrases.english: …so that it will delay (decay).
phrases.notes: End of the previous משנה sentence, which started on the prior page.

phrases.english: One may tie the jaw,
not so that it will rise back up,
but so that it will not open further.

steps.triggerLanguage: קוֹשְׁרִין אֶת הַלֶּחִי, לֹא שֶׁיַּעֲלֶה, אֶלָּא שֶׁלֹּא יוֹסִיף
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה's list of things allowed for a מת on שבת, from the previous page.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: You may tie a מת's jaw on שבת only to stop it from opening more, not to close it.

steps.title: Propping up a cracked roof beam, only to stop it from falling more
steps.stepSummary: Using the same principle, the משנה lets you support a cracked beam with a bench or bed poles. The goal must be stopping it from sagging more, not pushing it back up.
steps.simpleTranslation: And similarly, a beam that broke: we support it with a bench or with the long poles of a bed, not so that it will go up, but so that it will not get worse.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה applies the same rule to a different case. You may prop up a cracked roof beam on שבת, but only to keep it from falling further.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word וְכֵן ('and similarly') tells us this is the same principle as the jaw. Propping the beam to hold it in place is allowed. Raising it back into position looks like building or fixing, so that is not allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: the long side-poles of a bed

steps.whatToRemember: The rule in both משנה cases: on שבת you may stop something from getting worse, but you may not fix it.

phrases.english: And similarly, a beam that cracked —
we may support it with a bench
or with the long poles of a bed,
not so that it will rise back up,
but so that it will not sag further.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the jaw principle from Step 1 to a broken beam.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A cracked beam may be propped up to stop it from falling, not to restore it.

steps.title: Challenge: רבי מאיר forbade rinsing and oiling a floor
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the משנה's earlier permission to oil and rinse a מת. It quotes a story in which רבי מאיר forbade rinsing or oiling a bathhouse floor on שבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: But didn't רב יהודה say in the name of שמואל: There was a story with a student of רבי מאיר who went in after him to the bathhouse. He wanted to rinse the floor; רבי מאיר told him, 'We do not rinse.' He wanted to oil the floor; he told him, 'We do not oil.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins. It attacks the משנה's earlier ruling that you may oil and rinse a dead body. The source is a story where רבי מאיר forbade rinsing and oiling a floor on שבת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A floor and a dead body seem alike. Neither may be moved on שבת, and both are just being rinsed or oiled. So if rinsing and oiling a floor is forbidden, why is it allowed for a מת?

keyTerms.meaning: the Talmud's discussion of the משנה

steps.confusionAlert: This challenge is not aimed at the jaw or beam rules you just read. It targets an earlier line in the same משנה: 'סכין ומדיחין' (we oil and rinse the מת).

phrases.english: GEMARA:
But didn't Rav Yehuda say in the name of Shmuel:
There was an incident with a student of Rabbi Meir
who went in after him to the bathhouse,
he wanted to rinse the floor,
he said to him: We do not rinse.
(He wanted) to oil the floor,
he said to him: We do not oil.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts the גמרא. It returns to the משנה's earlier ruling about oiling and rinsing a מת.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling 'סכין ומדיחין את המת' (we may oil and rinse a dead body on שבת).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי מאיר forbade rinsing and oiling a floor on שבת. A body seems similar, so rinsing and oiling it should also be forbidden.

steps.title: Answer: a floor can be confused with a dirt floor, but a body cannot
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the floor case is a special worry. A tiled floor can be mistaken for a dirt floor, and smoothing a dirt floor is a real problem. A body will never be mistaken for a floor.
steps.simpleTranslation: Floor with floor — people confuse them. A dead body with a floor — people do not confuse them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. It shows that the floor rule comes from a special concern that does not apply to a body.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Rinsing even a tiled floor was forbidden because someone might do the same to a dirt floor. That would smooth out its holes, which is a real שבת problem. A body looks nothing like a floor, so there is no worry of confusion, and rinsing and oiling a body stays permitted.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a classic גזירה pattern. Something permitted is forbidden only when it can be mistaken for something truly forbidden. Where there is no confusion, there is no גזירה.

phrases.english: Floor with floor — they get confused,
a body with a floor — it does not get confused.

steps.triggerLanguage: קַרְקַע בְּקַרְקַע מִחַלְּפָא, מֵת בְּקַרְקַע לָא מִיחַלַּף
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction between cases (חילוק): the risk of confusion exists for a floor but not for a body.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Rinsing or oiling anything that may not be moved on שבת is forbidden, floor and body alike.
steps.terutzMaskana: The floor rule is only a גזירה against confusing it with a dirt floor. A מת cannot be confused with a floor, so oiling and rinsing it is permitted.

steps.title: What does the word 'all' add?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what extra case the משנה's word ״כל״ comes to include, in the phrase 'we do all the needs of the dead.'
steps.simpleTranslation: 'All' — what does it come to include?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to a new point in the משנה. It asks what the word 'all' adds. This sets up the next step, which gives the answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה said 'עושין כל צרכי המת,' we do all the needs of the dead. The גמרא assumes the extra word 'all' is there to teach a case we would not have known otherwise.

phrases.english: 'All' — to include what?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new question about a different phrase in the משנה. It is not connected to the floor discussion.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which extra case the word ״כל״ in 'כל צרכי המת' comes to include.

steps.title: 'All' includes cooling the stomach and sealing the body's openings
steps.stepSummary: The word ״כל״ includes a ברייתא. You may place cool or metal vessels on the body's stomach so it won't swell, and you may plug its openings so air won't get in.
steps.simpleTranslation: To include what the Rabbis taught: We bring cooling vessels and metal vessels and place them on its stomach so that it won't swell. And we plug its openings so that air won't enter them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from Step 5. 'All' includes extra steps to keep the body from swelling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These actions go beyond the oiling and rinsing the משנה listed. Laying cool vessels on the stomach slows swelling, and plugging the openings keeps air out. The word 'all' tells us these are also allowed on שבת.
steps.whatToRemember: ״כל צרכי המת״ is broad. It also includes steps to prevent swelling: cool or metal vessels on the stomach, and sealing the body's openings.

phrases.english: To include that which the Rabbis taught:
We bring a cooling vessel
and metal vessels,
and place them on its stomach
so that it will not swell.
And we plug its openings
so that air will not enter them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in Step 5.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: ״כל״ includes placing cool or metal vessels on the stomach and plugging the body's openings to prevent swelling.

steps.title: שלמה המלך's verse describing the body breaking down
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a verse from קהלת by שלמה המלך. It reads each image as a body part that fails at death, including the stomach (the 'pitcher') bursting. This fits the concern about the stomach swelling.
steps.simpleTranslation: And שלמה also said in his wisdom: 'Before the silver cord is snapped' — this is the spinal cord. 'And the golden bowl is shattered' — this is the male organ. 'And the pitcher is broken at the fountain' — this is the stomach. 'And the wheel falls into the pit' — this is excrement.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a verse from קהלת. It shows that שלמה המלך also described how the body breaks down, including the stomach bursting.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each image in the verse is read as a body part. The 'pitcher broken at the fountain' is the stomach, which swells and bursts after death. That links to the previous step about preventing swelling. The word וְאַף ('and also') marks this as extra support, not a new law.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't look for a new הלכה here. This is an aggadic, descriptive passage that backs up the idea that the body, especially the stomach, breaks down after death.

phrases.english: And Solomon also said in his wisdom:
'Before the silver cord is snapped' —
this is the spinal cord.
'And the golden bowl is shattered' —
this is the male organ.
'And the pitcher is broken at the fountain' —
this is the stomach.
'And the wheel falls shattered into the pit' —
this is excrement.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds verse-based support to Step 6's concern about the stomach swelling and bursting.
steps.raayaObject: The idea that the body, especially the stomach, swells and breaks down after death.
steps.raayaSupportSource: קהלת 12:6, read as describing body parts failing at death.

steps.title: A second verse about the stomach after death
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא adds a verse from מלאכי about 'dung on your faces' as more support for the idea that the stomach fails after death.
steps.simpleTranslation: And similarly it says: 'And I will spread dung upon your faces, the dung of your festivals.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second verse that also hints at what happens to the stomach after death. It is building on the קהלת verse from the step before.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase 'dung upon your faces' sounds like the contents of the stomach ending up on the person's face. The next two steps explain who the verse is talking about and how it actually happens.

keyTerms.meaning: And similarly it says (adds another verse with the same idea)
Dung, the waste inside the stomach

phrases.english: And similarly it says:
"And I will spread dung upon your faces,
the dung of your festivals."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second verse that supports the same idea as the קהלת verse in step 7.
steps.raayaObject: The idea that the stomach bursts and fails after death
steps.raayaSupportSource: מלאכי ב:ג, 'And I will spread dung upon your faces'

steps.title: Who the verse in מלאכי is talking about
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא (or רב חגא) explains that the verse refers to people who leave Torah learning and treat every day like a holiday.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא said, and some say it was רב חגא who said: These are people who leave the words of Torah and make all their days like festivals.
steps.whatsHappening: An אמורא explains the word 'your festivals' in the verse. It describes people who neglect Torah and spend every day feasting as if it were a holiday.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This explains why the verse says 'the dung of your festivals.' The food these people ate during their endless 'holidays' is the same waste that will later end up on their faces. It turns the verse into a moral warning, not just a description of the body.

keyTerms.meaning: They leave or neglect Torah learning
Like festivals, meaning days of eating and partying

phrases.english: Rav Huna said,
and some say Rav Chagga said:
These are people
who leave the words of Torah,
and make all their days like festivals.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא וְאָמְרִי לַהּ אָמַר רַב חַגָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the word 'festivals' in the verse quoted in step 8.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The verse in מלאכי refers to people who neglect Torah and treat every day like a feast day.

steps.title: The stomach bursts three days after death
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע says that three days after death the stomach bursts, falls onto the face, and says 'Take what you put in me.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי לוי said that רב פפי said that רבי יהושע said: After three days, the stomach bursts, falls onto the person's face, and says to him, 'Take what you put into me.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע describes exactly how the 'dung upon your faces' happens. After three days the stomach bursts and spills onto the face.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This connects the verse to a real physical event, which fits the earlier worry about the stomach swelling (step 6). The stomach 'speaking' is a sharp rebuke: the food you stuffed into me is now yours to take back.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי לֵוִי אָמַר רַב פַּפֵּי
phrases.english: Rabbi Levi said that Rav Pappi said
that Rabbi Yehoshua said:
After three days
his stomach bursts
and falls onto his face,
and says to him:
"Take what you put into me."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי לֵוִי אָמַר רַב פַּפֵּי אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows how the verse from step 8 actually happens to the body.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Three days after death the stomach bursts and spills onto the face.
steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא let us put cool vessels on the stomach so it won't swell (step 6). The verses from קהלת and מלאכי, and רבי יהושע's description, all show that the stomach really does swell and burst after death.

steps.title: The משנה: Do not close the eyes of the dying
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that we may not close a dead person's eyes on שבת, and on any day we may not close them while the person is still dying, since that counts as killing.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: We do not close the eyes of a dead person on שבת. And even on a weekday we do not close them while the soul is leaving. Whoever closes the eyes while the soul is leaving is like someone who sheds blood.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins with two rules about closing a person's eyes at death. On שבת it is not allowed at all, and on any day it is forbidden while the person is still in the process of dying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On שבת the body is מוקצה, so we may not move the eyelids. On a weekday the problem is different: touching a dying person can speed up death, so the משנה calls it שופך דמים.

keyTerms.meaning: The soul leaving, the moments of dying
One who sheds blood, a murderer

steps.confusionAlert: מְעַצְּמִין here means closing the eyes, not anything to do with bones (עֶצֶם). The root comes from the eyes being shut tight, as in 'עוֹצֵם עֵינָיו'.

phrases.english: MISHNAH:
We do not close the eyes of the dead on Shabbat,
and not on a weekday while the soul is leaving.
And one who closes the eyes while the soul is leaving —
this person is a shedder of blood.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ אֵין מְעַצְּמִין אֶת הַמֵּת בַּשַּׁבָּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה. It moves from the aggadic stomach discussion back to practical laws about the dead.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No closing a dead person's eyes on שבת. On any day, no closing the eyes of someone who is still dying, because that hastens death.

steps.title: The candle parable
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא repeats the משנה's ruling and explains it with a parable of a flickering candle snuffed out by a finger.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: The רבנן taught: Whoever closes the eyes while the soul is leaving is a shedder of blood. It is like a candle that is slowly going out. If a person puts his finger on it, it goes out right away.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא that gives the reason behind the משנה's harsh language. It uses a picture of a candle to explain why closing the eyes counts as killing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A dying candle could still burn a little longer, but a finger ends it at once. In the same way, a dying person still has some life left, and touching him can cut that life short. So even a small act counts as taking a life.

keyTerms.meaning: A candle that is slowly going out

steps.whyThisMatters: This parable is the classic source for the הלכה that a גוסס (a person in the final stage of dying) must not be touched or moved in a way that could speed up death.

phrases.english: GEMARA: The Rabbis taught:
One who closes his eyes while the soul is leaving —
this person is a shedder of blood.
It is like a candle that is slowly going out,
if a person puts his finger on it —
it goes out immediately.

steps.triggerLanguage: גְּמָ׳ תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן הַמְעַצְּמוֹ עִם יְצִיאַת הַנֶּפֶשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reason for the משנה's ruling in step 11.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Closing the eyes of a dying person is like snuffing out a candle that was about to go out; it shortens life and counts as killing.

steps.title: How to close the eyes without touching them
steps.stepSummary: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל gives a method that makes a dead person's eyes close on their own.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: Someone who wants a dead person's eyes to close should blow wine into his nose, put oil between his eyelids, and hold his two big toes, and the eyes will close by themselves.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא with a practical tip. It shows how to get the eyes of a dead person to close naturally without pressing them shut.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This method is for after death, not while the person is dying. It lets the eyes shut on their own, without pressing them closed by hand.

phrases.aramaic: תַּנְיָא, רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: It was taught: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
One who wants the eyes of a dead person to close —
should blow wine into his nose,
and put oil between his eyelids,
and hold his two big toes,
and they (the eyes) close by themselves.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא, רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר: הָרוֹצֶה שֶׁיִּתְעַצְּמוּ עֵינָיו שֶׁל מֵת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After forbidding forced eye-closing, the גמרא gives a gentle, natural way to close the eyes after death.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A dead person's eyes can be made to close on their own with wine in the nose, oil on the eyelids, and holding the big toes.

steps.title: A living baby versus a dead king
steps.stepSummary: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל teaches that we break שבת for a one-day-old living baby, but not for the body of דוד המלך.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: For a living one-day-old baby, we break שבת. For דוד, king of Israel, once he is dead, we do not break שבת.
steps.whatsHappening: Since the topic is the dead, the גמרא brings a related ברייתא. It sets up a surprising contrast that the next step will explain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The contrast is meant to be shocking: a tiny baby gets more than the greatest king. The point is that what matters is being alive, not greatness. The reason is given in the next step.

phrases.aramaic: תַּנְיָא, רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: It was taught: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
A living one-day-old baby —
we break Shabbat for him;
David, king of Israel, dead —
we do not break Shabbat for him.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא, רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר: תִּינוֹק בֶּן יוֹמוֹ חַי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A related teaching brought because the discussion is about the dead. It opens a new topic: when we break שבת for a person.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: We break שבת to save a living baby, even one day old, but not for the body of even the greatest dead person.

steps.title: Why the baby comes before the king
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא explains: the baby will keep many שבתות in the future, while a dead person no longer has any מצוות.
steps.simpleTranslation: For a living one-day-old baby we break שבת, because the Torah said: Break one שבת for him so that he will keep many שבתות. For דוד, king of Israel, once dead, we do not break שבת, because once a person dies he is released from the מצוות.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא repeats both cases and gives the reason for each. This explains the surprising contrast from the last step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Breaking שבת for the baby is worth it because it leads to more שבת keeping later. A dead person can never keep מצוות again, so there is nothing to gain by breaking שבת for him. That is why greatness does not matter here, only life.

keyTerms.meaning: Released from, no longer doing, the מצוות

phrases.english: A living one-day-old baby —
we break Shabbat for him,
because the Torah said:
Break one Shabbat for him,
so that he will keep many Shabbatot.
David, king of Israel, dead —
we do not break Shabbat for him,
because once a person dies
he is released from the מצוות.

steps.triggerLanguage: תִּינוֹק בֶּן יוֹמוֹ חַי מְחַלְּלִין עָלָיו אֶת הַשַּׁבָּת, אָמְרָה תּוֹרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Repeats the two cases from step 14 in order to explain the reason behind each.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the reason behind a surprising contrast
steps.terutzHavaAmina: One might think a great king deserves more than a tiny baby.
steps.terutzMaskana: What counts is future מצוות: the baby will keep many שבתות, but a dead person is free from all מצוות.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: We break שבת for a living baby because he will keep many שבתות. We do not break it for a dead person, because once a person dies he is released from the מצוות.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: the dead are free from מצוות
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא connects the ברייתא's reason to רבי יוחנן's reading of 'במתים חפשי,' meaning the dead are free from מצוות.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this is what רבי יוחנן said: 'Among the dead, free' — once a person dies, he becomes free from the מצוות.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that the ברייתא's idea matches what רבי יוחנן taught from a verse in תהלים. This closes the discussion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא said a dead person is released from מצוות. רבי יוחנן finds this in the words 'במתים חפשי': 'free' means free from מצוות. So the reason now has a verse behind it.

keyTerms.meaning: And this is what (so-and-so) said, linking two teachings

steps.whatToRemember: We break שבת to save any living person, even a one-day-old baby, because that person will keep many מצוות later. We do not break שבת for a dead body, even of דוד המלך, because a dead person is free from מצוות, as רבי יוחנן learns from 'במתים חפשי.'

phrases.english: And this is what Rabbi Yochanan said:
"Among the dead, free" —
once a person dies,
he becomes free from the מצוות.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the reason given in step 15 with רבי יוחנן's reading of a verse.
steps.raayaObject: The idea that once a person dies he is released from מצוות
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יוחנן's reading of תהלים פח:ו, 'במתים חפשי'

steps.title: Animals fear a living baby but not a dead giant
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר teaches that a living one-day-old baby needs no guarding from weasels and mice, but even the dead עוג מלך הבשן does.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught in a ברייתא: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר says: A living one-day-old baby does not need to be guarded from a weasel or from mice. But עוג, king of בשן, once dead, does need to be guarded from a weasel and from mice.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another ברייתא that continues the theme of how special a living person is, even a tiny baby.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Animals stay away from a living person, even a helpless newborn. Once someone dies, even the mighty giant עוג, animals are no longer afraid of him. This continues the contrast from the previous steps between the living baby and the dead.

keyTerms.meaning: עוג, the giant king of בשן

phrases.aramaic: תַּנְיָא, רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: It was taught in a baraita: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says:
A one-day-old baby who is alive —
does not need to be guarded
from the weasel or from the mice.
phrases.notes: The animals run away from a living person on their own.

phrases.english: But Og, king of Bashan, once dead —
needs to be guarded
from the weasel and from the mice,

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא, רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another ברייתא with the same living-versus-dead contrast as the baby versus דוד המלך teaching.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Animals fear a living person, even a newborn, but do not fear a dead person, even עוג.

steps.title: The verse showing animals fear only the living
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא proves its point from the פסוק 'ומוראכם וחתכם יהיה', reading חתכם as 'your being alive'.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it says: 'And your fear and your dread shall be' upon all animals. As long as a person is alive, the fear of him lies upon the creatures. Once he dies, the fear of him is gone.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives a פסוק as the source for why animals fear only living people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word וחתכם ('your dread') is read as if it said 'your life' (חיתכם, from חי, alive). So the fear that animals have of people depends on the person being alive. Once a person dies, that fear disappears.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Your fear and your dread' (from the פסוק in בראשית)

steps.confusionAlert: The proof does not come from the simple meaning 'dread'. It comes from reading חתכם as connected to חי, 'alive'.

phrases.english: as it is stated: "And the fear of you and the dread of you shall be",
phrases.notes: בראשית ט:ב — the verse continues 'upon every beast of the earth'.

phrases.english: as long as a person is alive —
phrases.notes: The word חתכם is read as hinting at חי, 'alive'.

phrases.english: the fear of him lies upon the creatures;
once he dies — the fear of him is gone.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the פסוק source for the ruling in step 17.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that animals fear only living people.
steps.raayaSupportSource: בראשית ט:ב, 'ומוראכם וחתכם יהיה', with חתכם read as 'your being alive'.

steps.title: A lion does not attack two people
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא states a known tradition: a lion does not pounce on two people together.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: We have a tradition: a lion does not pounce on two people.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא adds another teaching about animals and people: two people together are safe from a lion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This continues the theme that animals naturally fear people. רב פפא presents it as an accepted tradition ('we hold'). The next step will challenge it from real life.

keyTerms.meaning: We have a tradition / we hold

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said: We hold:
a lion does not pounce upon two people.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shifts to a related teaching about when animals attack people.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A lion does not attack two people together.

steps.title: But we see lions do attack two
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב פפא: we can see with our own eyes that lions do attack two people.
steps.simpleTranslation: But we see that it does pounce!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב פפא's tradition from what people actually see happen.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If lions never attack two people, how do we explain real cases where they do? Real life seems to disprove the tradition.

phrases.english: But we see that it does pounce?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רב פפא's statement in step 19.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב פפא's claim that a lion does not attack two people.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Experience shows lions sometimes do attack two people, which contradicts the tradition.

steps.title: Animals attack only people who seem like animals
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers with רמי בר אבא: an animal only overpowers a person who appears to it like an animal, as the פסוק in תהלים says.
steps.simpleTranslation: That case follows רמי בר אבא. For רמי בר אבא said: An animal does not overpower a person until he seems to it like an animal, as it says: 'A person in honor does not last; he is compared to the animals that perish.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge: when a lion does attack two people, it is because those people seem like animals to it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב פפא's rule holds for people who keep their human dignity. A person who lowers himself spiritually loses that protection and looks like an animal to the beast. So the attacks we see are exceptions, and the rule still stands.

keyTerms.meaning: Appears to it like an animal
'A person in honor does not last' (תהלים מט)

phrases.english: That case is in line with Rami bar Abba.
For Rami bar Abba said:
An animal does not overpower a person
until he appears to it like an animal,
as it is stated: "But man does not abide in honor,
he is like the beasts that perish."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 20.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the cases: the attacks we see happen only to people who appear animal-like.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Lions attacking two people disproves רב פפא's tradition.
steps.terutzMaskana: The rule holds for people who keep their human dignity. Those who lower themselves look like animals and can be attacked.

steps.title: Do not sleep alone in a house
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא teaches that it is forbidden to sleep alone in a house, because a person sleeping alone may be seized by לילית.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנינא said: It is forbidden to sleep alone in a house, and anyone who sleeps alone in a house is seized by לילית.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a related warning about danger: being alone, like the lone person a lion might attack, is risky.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This fits the theme of רב פפא: there is safety in numbers. Here the danger is a harmful spirit, לילית, instead of a wild animal.

phrases.english: Rabbi Hanina said:
It is prohibited to sleep alone in a house,
and anyone who sleeps alone in a house —
Lilith seizes him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי חֲנִינָא: אָסוּר לִישַׁן בַּבַּיִת יְחִידִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A similar teaching: being alone brings danger, as with the lion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: It is forbidden to sleep alone in a house because of danger from לילית.

steps.title: Do מצוות while you still can
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר urges doing מצוות while you have the opportunity, the money, and control over yourself.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר says: Do מצוות while you can find the chance, while you have the means, and while you are still in control of yourself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the theme of valuing life, which started with the baby who will keep many שבתות. A living person should use his life to do מצוות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are three things a person may lose: the opportunity, the money, and his own strength or control. Since these can disappear, a person should not delay doing מצוות.

keyTerms.meaning: You are still in your own control

phrases.aramaic: תַּנְיָא, רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: It was taught in a baraita: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says:
Perform מצוות while you still find the opportunity,
and you have the means, and you are still in your own control.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא, רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר אוֹמֵר: עֲשֵׂה עַד שֶׁאַתָּה מוֹצֵא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the theme that life is the time for מצוות.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Do מצוות now, while opportunity, means, and strength are still available.

steps.title: שלמה's verse about remembering God in youth
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא supports its point with the פסוק in קהלת, explaining 'evil days' as old age and 'years with no desire' as the days of משיח, when there is no merit or liability.
steps.simpleTranslation: And שלמה also said in his wisdom: 'Remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the evil days come' — these are the days of old age. 'And the years arrive when you will say, I have no desire for them' — these are the days of משיח, when there is neither merit nor liability.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא brings a פסוק from שלמה to back up the advice to do מצוות early.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two times will come when doing מצוות is harder or worth less. In old age, a person is weak. In the days of משיח, according to this view, there is no merit or liability, so there is no chance to earn reward. Therefore a person should act now.

phrases.english: And Solomon too said in his wisdom:
"And remember your Creator in the days of your youth
before the evil days come" —
these are the days of old age;

phrases.aramaic: ״וְהִגִּיעוּ שָׁנִים אֲשֶׁר תֹּאמַר אֵין לִי בָהֶם חֵפֶץ״ —
phrases.english: "and the years arrive when you will say: I have no desire for them" —
these are the days of the Messiah,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאֵין בָּהֶם לֹא זְכוּת וְלֹא חוֹבָה.
phrases.english: in which there is neither merit nor liability.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a פסוק as support for the advice in step 23.
steps.raayaObject: The advice to do מצוות while one still can.
steps.raayaSupportSource: קהלת יב:א, read as referring to old age and to the days of משיח.

steps.title: שמואל sees the days of משיח differently
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that this reading disagrees with שמואל, who holds that the only difference in the days of משיח is freedom from foreign rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this disagrees with שמואל. For שמואל said: The only difference between this world and the days of משיח is being ruled by foreign kingdoms, as it says: 'For the poor will never cease from the land.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that the ברייתא's reading of the days of משיח argues with שמואל's view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא said the days of משיח will have no merit or liability, a totally changed world. שמואל says the world stays the same, including poor people who need צדקה, so there are still מצוות to earn merit. The only change is that we will be freed from foreign rule.
steps.whatToRemember: Life is the time to do מצוות. According to the ברייתא, even the days of משיח will not offer that chance. שמואל disagrees and holds that the world will stay as it is, except that we will be free of foreign rule.
steps.confusionAlert: שמואל is not denying that משיח will come. He only says that daily life, including poverty and מצוות, will continue as it is now.

phrases.english: And this disagrees with Shmuel,
for Shmuel said:

phrases.aramaic: אֵין בֵּין הָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה לִימוֹת הַמָּשִׁיחַ
phrases.english: There is no difference between this world and the days of the Messiah
except subjugation to foreign kingdoms alone,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: כִּי ״לֹא יֶחְדַּל אֶבְיוֹן מִקֶּרֶב הָאָרֶץ״.
phrases.english: as it is stated: "For the poor will never cease from the land."
phrases.notes: דברים טו:יא — poverty, and so the מצוה of צדקה, continues forever.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that the reading in step 24 is a disputed view, opposed by שמואל.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The ברייתא's view of the days of משיח disagrees with שמואל, who says the only change is freedom from foreign rule.

steps.title: Always pray not to become poor
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר הקפר teaches that a person should always ask for mercy about poverty, because if it does not reach him, it may reach his son or grandson.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא teaches: רבי אלעזר הקפר says a person should always pray for mercy about this condition of poverty. If he does not become poor, his son might. If his son does not, his grandson might.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new teaching from a ברייתא: pray about poverty, because it can reach your family down the line.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No family is safe from poverty forever. Even if you are wealthy now, your children or grandchildren may fall into it. So prayer about poverty is never pointless.

phrases.english: It was taught: Rabbi Elazar HaKappar says:
A person should always ask for mercy
about this condition (poverty),
phrases.notes: This picks up שמואל's verse just quoted, 'the poor will never cease from the land' (דברים 15:11).

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאִם הוּא לֹא בָּא — בָּא בְּנוֹ,
phrases.english: for if he does not come to it, his son will,

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם בְּנוֹ לֹא בָּא — בֶּן בְּנוֹ בָּא,
phrases.english: and if his son does not come to it, his grandson will,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Picks up the theme of poverty raised by שמואל's verse 'לא יחדל אביון' in step 25. The verse it quotes next, 'כי בגלל הדבר הזה' (דברים 15:10), sits right beside that verse.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person should always pray for mercy regarding poverty, since it may come to him or his descendants.

steps.title: The פסוק 'because of this thing'
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר הקפר supports his teaching with the פסוק 'כי בגלל הדבר הזה'.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it says: 'For because of this thing...'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא quotes a פסוק as the source for the idea that poverty moves around. The next line will explain how the פסוק teaches this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק is about giving צדקה to the poor. On its own the proof is not yet clear. The connection depends on the word 'בגלל', which the next step explains.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is said (introduces a פסוק)

phrases.english: as it is said: 'For because of this thing.'
phrases.notes: דברים 15:10, about giving to the poor.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the פסוק behind רבי אלעזר הקפר's statement.
steps.raayaObject: That poverty can come to oneself or one's descendants.

steps.title: Poverty is a wheel that turns
steps.stepSummary: The school of רבי ישמעאל explains 'בגלל' to mean that poverty is a wheel turning in the world.
steps.simpleTranslation: The school of רבי ישמעאל taught: It is a wheel that turns in the world.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains how the פסוק proves the point. 'בגלל' hints at 'גלגל', a wheel.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A wheel keeps turning, so whoever is on top now may later be at the bottom. Today's giver may be tomorrow's receiver, which is why one should give generously.

keyTerms.meaning: A תנא of the school of רבי ישמעאל taught
That turns around in the world

steps.whatToRemember: 'בגלל' = 'גלגל': wealth and poverty rotate between people.

phrases.english: The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught:
It is a wheel that turns in the world.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנָא דְּבֵי רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל: גַּלְגַּל הוּא שֶׁחוֹזֵר בָּעוֹלָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how the פסוק in step 27 teaches the idea.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'בגלל' teaches that poverty is a turning wheel in the world.

steps.title: A Torah scholar does not become poor
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף says there is a tradition that a צורבא מרבנן will not become poor.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: We have a tradition that a young Torah scholar does not become poor.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף adds a limit to the 'wheel': a תלמיד חכם is protected from poverty.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The wheel idea suggests anyone can become poor. רב יוסף claims Torah scholars are an exception. This claim will be challenged in the next step.

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said: We hold (by tradition):
A Torah scholar does not become poor.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds an exception to the 'wheel' of poverty.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A תלמיד חכם does not become poor.

steps.title: But we see scholars who are poor
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב יוסף: we see with our own eyes that Torah scholars do become poor.
steps.simpleTranslation: But we see that they do become poor!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רב יוסף's statement from real life: there are poor Torah scholars.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יוסף's tradition seems to clash with what everyone can observe. If scholars really are poor, what does his tradition mean?

keyTerms.meaning: But we see (a challenge from reality)

phrases.english: But we see that they do become poor!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב יוסף's tradition.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יוסף's claim that a תלמיד חכם does not become poor.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Observation: Torah scholars clearly are sometimes poor.

steps.title: He will not have to beg at doors
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers: even if a scholar becomes poor, he will not be reduced to begging door to door.
steps.simpleTranslation: If it happens that he becomes poor, he still will not go around begging at doors.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא narrows רב יוסף's statement. It does not mean no poverty at all. It means no extreme, door-to-door begging.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The tradition is reinterpreted. A scholar may lack money, but he is spared the deepest humiliation of poverty. This makes the tradition fit what we see.

phrases.english: If it is so that he becomes poor,
he does not go around begging at doors.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִם אִיתָא דְּמִיעֲנֵי, אַהְדּוֹרֵי אַפִּתְחָא לָא מַהְדַּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 30.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the meaning of the original statement.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב יוסף meant scholars never become poor at all.
steps.terutzMaskana: He meant scholars will never be reduced to begging door to door.

steps.title: רבי חייא tells his wife to feed the poor quickly
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא tells his wife to hurry and give bread to a poor person, so that others will hurry to give bread to her children.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חייא said to his wife: When a poor person comes, be quick to give him bread, so that others will be quick to give bread to your children.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a story that applies the 'wheel' idea in real life.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי חייא assumes his own children might one day need help. By helping the poor now, his wife earns that others will help their children later.

phrases.english: Rabbi Chiya said to his wife:

phrases.aramaic: כִּי אָתֵי עַנְיָא — אַקְדִּימִי לֵיהּ רִיפְתָּא,
phrases.english: When a poor person comes, be quick to give him bread,
so that they will be quick to give to your children.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A practical story applying the 'wheel' idea.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Give quickly to the poor so that your children will be helped quickly if they are in need.

steps.title: His wife objects: Are you cursing them?
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא's wife protests that his words sound like a curse that their children will become poor.
steps.simpleTranslation: She said to him: Are you cursing them?!
steps.whatsHappening: His wife challenges him: talking about their children needing bread sounds like wishing poverty on them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His words imply the children will one day be poor. She sees that as a curse, a bad sign spoken aloud.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַרָה לֵיהּ: מֵילָט קָא לָיְיטַתְּ לְהוּ?!
phrases.english: She said to him: Are you cursing them?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַרָה לֵיהּ: מֵילָט קָא לָיְיטַתְּ לְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Objection to רבי חייא's words.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי חייא's statement implying the children will need bread.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Saying your children will need charity sounds like cursing them.

steps.title: It is not a curse; it is a פסוק
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא answers that he is only repeating the פסוק and the teaching that poverty is a turning wheel.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to her: A פסוק is written: 'For because of this thing,' and the school of רבי ישמעאל taught: It is a wheel that turns in the world.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חייא explains he is not cursing. He is stating a fact taught by the Torah: wealth and poverty rotate.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the 'wheel' is a reality, preparing for it is wisdom, not a curse. Giving now protects one's descendants later.

phrases.english: He said to her: A verse is written:
'For because of this thing,'
and the school of Rabbi Yishmael taught:
It is a wheel that turns in the world.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the wife's objection.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reframing: the statement is a Torah fact, not a curse.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Talking about one's children needing bread is a curse.
steps.terutzMaskana: It is recognizing the 'wheel' that the Torah teaches, and acting wisely because of it.

steps.title: Whoever shows compassion receives compassion
steps.stepSummary: רבי גמליאל ברבי learns from a פסוק that Heaven shows compassion to whoever shows compassion to others.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא teaches: רבי גמליאל, son of רבי, says: 'And He will give you mercy, and have compassion on you, and multiply you.' Whoever has compassion on people receives compassion from Heaven. Whoever does not have compassion on people does not receive compassion from Heaven.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another teaching on the same theme: how you treat others decides how Heaven treats you.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק first says 'He will give you mercy' (you will become merciful), then 'and have compassion on you'. The order teaches cause and effect: being merciful leads to receiving mercy.
steps.whatToRemember: Measure for measure: showing compassion to others brings compassion from Heaven.

phrases.english: It was taught: Rabbi Gamliel son of Rabbi says:
'And He will give you mercy, and have compassion on you, and multiply you,'
whoever has compassion on people
receives compassion from Heaven,
and whoever does not have compassion on people
does not receive compassion from Heaven.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another teaching on the same theme of kindness to the poor.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One who has compassion on others receives compassion from Heaven, and one who does not, does not.

steps.title: Reading the images of old age as parts of the face
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to קהלת and explains the sun, light, moon, stars and clouds as parts of the body that weaken in old age.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Before the sun and the light are darkened': this is the forehead and the nose. 'And the moon': this is the soul. 'And the stars': these are the cheeks. 'And the clouds return after the rain': this is the light of a person's eyes, which fades after crying.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the פסוקים in קהלת about old age, which it began interpreting earlier. It explains each image as a part of the human face or body.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each heavenly light stands for something that 'shines' in a person and dims with age. The clouds after rain picture eyesight that fades after tears.
steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new topic. The גמרא is continuing its interpretation of קהלת 12, which it paused for the poverty discussion.

phrases.english: 'Before the sun and the light are darkened':
this is the forehead and the nose,
'and the moon': this is the soul,
'and the stars': these are the cheeks,
'and the clouds return after the rain':
this is the light of a person's eyes,
which fades after crying.

steps.triggerLanguage: עַד אֲשֶׁר לֹא תֶחְשַׁךְ הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ וְהָאוֹר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the קהלת interpretation from step 24.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The images in קהלת 12:2 refer to forehead, nose, soul, cheeks, and eyesight weakened by crying.

steps.title: Tears harm eyesight only after forty
steps.stepSummary: שמואל says that until age forty, eyesight recovers after crying. After forty it does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: Regarding tears, until forty years old the eyesight comes back. From then on it does not come back.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל adds detail to 'the clouds return after the rain.' Crying weakens the eyes for good only after age forty.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This explains why the פסוק links crying to old age. A young person's eyes recover from tears, but an older person's do not.

phrases.english: Shmuel said: Regarding tears,
until forty years, the eyesight returns;
from then on, it does not return.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Clarifies when crying harms eyesight.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Eyesight recovers from crying until forty, but not after.

steps.title: Eye shadow improves sight only until forty
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן says eye ointment improves vision until forty. After that, even a lot of it only keeps vision steady and does not improve it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said: Eye ointment (כוחלא) improves sight until forty years. From then on, even if one applies it as thick as a weaver's pin, it keeps the sight steady but does not improve it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן adds a similar rule about eye ointment. Forty is the turning point for the eyes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before forty the eyes can still get better. After forty, treatment can only stop them from getting worse. The 'weaver's pin' detail is puzzling, and the גמרא will ask about it next.

phrases.english: And Rav Nachman said: Eye ointment,
until forty years, improves sight;

phrases.aramaic: מִכָּאן וְאֵילָךְ — אֲפִילּוּ מְלֵי כְּאַכְסְנָא דְגַרְדָאֵי —
phrases.english: from then on, even if one applies it as thick as a weaver's pin,
it maintains the sight,
but it does not improve it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel teaching about the eyes at age forty.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Eye ointment improves sight until forty. After forty it only maintains it.

steps.title: What does the weaver's pin detail teach?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what רב נחמן is teaching by mentioning the thick weaver's pin.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is he teaching us?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why רב נחמן added the 'weaver's pin' detail. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The extra detail must carry a lesson. The גמרא wants to know what practical point it adds about how to use the ointment.

phrases.english: What is he teaching us?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the wording of רב נחמן's statement.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The lesson behind the phrase 'as thick as a weaver's pin.'

steps.title: The more ointment, the better
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the detail teaches that a thicker application of eye ointment is more helpful.
steps.simpleTranslation: That the more eye ointment one applies, the more beneficial it is.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question: the 'weaver's pin' teaches that applying more ointment helps more.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By saying 'even if it is as thick as a weaver's pin,' רב נחמן assumes that more ointment is normally better. Even so, after forty it cannot improve sight.
steps.whatToRemember: Forty is the turning point for the eyes: before it they recover and improve, after it they can only be maintained.

phrases.english: That the more thickly the eye ointment is applied,
the more beneficial it is.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 39.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The detail teaches that the more eye ointment one applies, the more it helps.

steps.title: רבי חנינא did not cry when his daughter died
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tells a story. רבי חנינא's daughter died, and he did not cry over her.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנינא's daughter died, and he did not cry over her.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a short story that ties into the earlier lines about crying and eyesight. It sets up the scene for the conversation that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story builds on step 37, where שמואל taught that after age forty, eyesight does not recover from crying. His silence looks cold, but the next steps show it comes from that concern about tears harming the eyes.

phrases.english: Rabbi Chanina's daughter died,
phrases.notes: Literally: 'his daughter lay down for him', a gentle way of saying she died.

phrases.english: he was not crying over her.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the discussion of eyesight and crying with a real-life story.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי חנינא did not cry at his daughter's death.

steps.title: His wife questions his lack of grief
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא's wife asks him sharply whether he thinks he just let a chicken out of the house, since he shows no sorrow.
steps.simpleTranslation: His wife said to him: Did you just let a chicken out of your house?!
steps.whatsHappening: His wife challenges him. She cannot understand why he acts as if he lost something small, like a chicken.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Her words are a rebuke, not a real question. She assumes his silence means he does not care, and this sets up his explanation in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: you let out, you sent out

phrases.english: His wife said to him:
Did you just let a chicken out of your house?!
phrases.notes: A rhetorical question meaning: you act as if you lost something worthless.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי חנינא's behavior described in step 41.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי חנינא's not crying over his daughter.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A loving father should grieve openly. Not crying looks as if he treats the loss as trivial.

steps.title: רבי חנינא explains: crying would be a double loss
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא answers that if he cries, he will suffer twice: once from losing his child and again from going blind.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to her: Two losses, being bereaved and being blind.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חנינא answers his wife. His grief is real, but crying would damage his eyes and add a second tragedy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He is not saying the loss is small. He is saying that crying would bring blindness on top of the bereavement, so he holds back his tears to protect his eyes.

phrases.english: He said to her: Two —
bereavement and blindness.
phrases.notes: If I cry, I will suffer both the loss of my child and the loss of my sight.

steps.confusionAlert: רבי חנינא is not saying he did not care. He grieved, but he avoided tears because they would harm his eyes.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the wife's challenge from step 42.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the hidden reason behind the behavior
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Not crying means he does not feel the loss.
steps.terutzMaskana: He avoids crying to protect his eyesight, so he does not suffer a second loss.

steps.title: Six kinds of tears: three good and three bad
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that רבי חנינא followed the teaching of רבי יוחנן in the name of רבי יוסי בן קצרתה: there are six kinds of tears, three good for the eyes and three harmful. The list begins with tears from smoke and from crying.
steps.simpleTranslation: He held like the teaching that רבי יוחנן said in the name of רבי יוסי בן קצרתה: There are six kinds of tears. Three are good and three are bad. Tears from smoke and from crying...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the source behind רבי חנינא's behavior. It starts listing the six kinds of tears, and the list continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This teaching gives a basis for רבי חנינא's fear of blindness. Some tears harm the eyes, and the list begins with smoke and crying from grief. The rest of the list, and which tears are good or bad, comes next.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that רבי חנינא's restraint came from a known teaching about health, not from coldness.

phrases.english: He held in accordance with this

phrases.aramaic: דַּאֲמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בֶּן קַצַּרְתָּה:
phrases.english: that Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Yosei ben Ketzarta:
There are six kinds of tears —
three are good, and three are bad.
Those from smoke, and those from crying,
phrases.notes: The list continues on the next amud.

steps.triggerLanguage: סָבַר לַהּ כִּי הָא דַּאֲמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for רבי חנינא's concern about blindness in step 43.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There are six kinds of tears, three good and three harmful. The list begins with tears from smoke and from crying.
